hints: Start by working out what solution Y actually is, sodium in water makes a very strong alkali, so think high pH.
For the pH to fall, substance X must remove $\text{OH}^-$ ions from that alkaline solution, either by precipitation or by reacting as an acid.
Check each compound for how it behaves with $\text{NaOH}$, a neutral salt does nothing and a basic oxide adds more alkali, so only the pair that both consume $\text{OH}^-$ will work.
walkthrough:
**Identify solution Y**

Great start, let's see what we have. Sodium is a very reactive Group 1 metal.

$$2\text{Na} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$$

So solution Y is sodium hydroxide, a strong alkali with a very high pH, around 13 to 14.

**Understand what pH fall means**

For the pH to fall, the concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ must decrease. That means X must use up $\text{OH}^-$ ions in a reaction.

**Test $\text{MgCl}_2$ with NaOH**

$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions form an insoluble hydroxide with $\text{OH}^-$. This removes $\text{OH}^-$ from solution as a precipitate.

$$\text{MgCl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{NaCl}$$

Less free $\text{OH}^-$ means the pH falls, so $\text{MgCl}_2$ works.

**Test $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ with NaOH**

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so it can react with both acids and strong alkalis. With excess $\text{NaOH}$ it dissolves to form an aluminate ion.

$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow [\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$$

Again $\text{OH}^-$ is consumed, so the pH falls. This also works.

**Conclude the pair**

Both $\text{MgCl}_2$ and $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ lower the $\text{OH}^-$ concentration and lower the pH. That matching pair is the answer.

options.A: Both compounds remove $\text{OH}^-$ from solution Y. $\text{MgCl}_2$ precipitates $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, and amphoteric $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ reacts to give $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$. In both cases $[\text{OH}^-]$ falls, so pH falls.
options.B: $\text{MgCl}_2$ does lower pH by precipitation, but $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ is a basic oxide. It reacts $\text{K}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{KOH}$, adding more $\text{OH}^-$ and raising pH, not lowering it.
options.C: $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ does lower pH, but $\text{NaCl}$ is a neutral salt from a strong acid and strong base. It does not react with $\text{NaOH}$, so pH stays the same. This is a common trap of thinking all chlorides behave like $\text{MgCl}_2$.
options.D: Neither works. $\text{NaCl}$ is neutral and has no effect on pH, while $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ forms extra $\text{KOH}$ and would increase $[\text{OH}^-]$, pushing pH up if anything.
